title: Other people's cows (15–20)
hookLine: one who recites much but doesn't act is like a cowherd counting others' cows (Dhammapada 19)

cards: A hired cowherd stands at the gate at the end of the day, counting cattle as they come in. Thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three. He knows every animal: which cow gives the most milk, which calf was born last spring.
But at the end of the season, not one drop of that milk is his. He's counting other people's cows.
The Dhammapada uses that picture for a very particular kind of person, someone who might be a lot like you and me, a few weeks into reading a book of wisdom.

teach.b: The chapter ends with three more twin pairs. Verses fifteen and sixteen: the one who does evil “mourns in this world, and he mourns in the next”; the one who does good delights in both.
Seventeen and eighteen say the same with suffering and happiness. Then nineteen and twenty, the cowherd.

Verse nineteen, in Müller's English: “The thoughtless man, even if he can recite a large portion (of the law), but is not a doer of it, has no share in the priesthood, but is like a cowherd counting the cows of others.”
Priesthood is Müller's word; the Pali means something like a share in the life of a seeker.

Verse twenty is the twin: someone who can recite only a little, but lets go of greed, hatred and delusion and lives it, has that share in full. The commentary tells it about two friends who became monks together.
One studied the scriptures and had many students. The other learned only a little, went off to the forest, meditated, and became fully awakened.

teach.h: THE SCHOLAR AND THE QUIET FRIEND.
teach.b: When the scholar came to test his friend with hard questions, the Buddha asked them both about the deeper stages of the path, and only the quiet one could answer.
So look back at chapter one. The mind comes first, manopubbangama. Hatred ends by not-hatred.
Thatch the roof. And now: none of it is yours by being counted. Knowing verses is fine; it's what these lessons are made of.
But the verse you live today outweighs the ten you can recite.

how: Theravada teachers pair study with practice, and some cite the cowherd verse to warn that reciting scripture is not the same as living it.

o: riches you envy that belong to your neighbors, not you
verses you recite but don't live, so they're not yours
duties that belong to others, so you can leave them alone

games.q: match the pieces of verses fifteen to twenty.
p: mourns in this world and the next
learned a little and lived it

s: the Dhammapada says studying the texts is worthless
verse twenty praises someone who knows only a little and lives it; the point is living, not ignorance.
in the commentary, the monk who meditated in the forest could answer the deeper questions
the scholar could not, though he had many students.
'priesthood' in Müller's verse nineteen is an exact match for the Pali
the Pali means a share in the life of a seeker or recluse.

games.q: your friend became a well-known scholar. you learned a little and went to meditate in the forest. now he comes to test you with hard questions. what does the story say happened?
o: you were embarrassed and couldn't answer.
the Buddha asked you both about the path, and only you could answer the deeper questions.
games.why: in the commentary, the Buddha himself asked the questions, and the quiet friend who had lived the teaching answered them.

practice: Let chapter one's four lines pass by once, like cattle through a gate: the wheel follows the ox, hatred ends by not-hatred, thatch the roof, not someone else's cows.
Choose just one, not the one that sounds wisest but the one you could actually live in the life you have, and hold it for a few breaths, picturing one moment later today when you might use it.
Then let it go and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Other people's cows. Knowing many verses without living them is counting cattle that aren't yours; living a few makes them your own.

orig.note: Pali: cowherd, the one counting others' cows in verse nineteen.

carryVoice: Your line: not someone else's cows. Chapter one, all the way through. That's day one hundred sixty-one.
